    Crossing two databases

    Source: vignettes/articles/crossing-two-databases.Rmd
    crossing-two-databases.Rmd

    This guide is the English version of 12. Cruzar dos bases. lupa writes its messages and tables in Spanish, so the output below is in Spanish.

    A registry lives in one SQLite database. The visits live in a DuckDB database. The credential that opens one does not open the other, and no query can name both at once. How do you know whether every visit finds its person? And how do you turn that question into a measure that can be repeated for every delivery?

    In this guide:

    • profiling each table in its engine with perfilar_dbi();
    • reading only the keys, in blocks, with DBI::dbSendQuery() and DBI::dbFetch();
    • comparing the coverage in R with detectar_relaciones();
    • turning the comparison into a metric with medir() and ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad;
    • deciding what to do when the keys do not have the same type or the same shape.

    Two databases, one question

    The example has 8 people in the registry and 20 visits. The visits store the person as a 2-digit text with a leading zero. Two visits cite people 9 and 10, who are not in the registry. Everything is synthetic.

    library(lupa)

padron <- data.frame(
  id_persona = 1:8,
  sector = rep(c("Norte", "Sur"), each = 4),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
visitas <- data.frame(
  id_visita = 1:20,
  id_persona = sprintf("%02d", c(rep(1:8, 2), 1, 2, 9, 10)),
  motivo = rep(c("control", "consulta"), length.out = 20),
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
head(visitas, 3)
#>   id_visita id_persona   motivo
#> 1         1         01  control
#> 2         2         02 consulta
#> 3         3         03  control

    The tables are written to in-memory databases. This only prepares the example: lupa does not write to the database.

    con_padron <- DBI::dbConnect(RSQLite::SQLite(), ":memory:")
DBI::dbWriteTable(con_padron, "padron", padron)
con_visitas <- suppressMessages(DBI::dbConnect(duckdb::duckdb()))
DBI::dbWriteTable(con_visitas, "visitas", visitas)

    Profiling each table in its engine

    Each table is profiled with the connection that sees it. perfilar_dbi() returns the 2 blocks of Profiling a database: the summary computed by the engine and the profile of the rows that were read.

    perfil_padron <- perfilar_dbi(con_padron, "padron")
perfil_visitas <- perfilar_dbi(con_visitas, "visitas")

    For the cross, only one thing in the profile matters: how the key is stored. The declared type is reported by the engine; the inferred one comes from the rows that were read.

    clave_de <- function(perfil, columna) {
  fila <- perfil$perfil_muestra$columnas
  fila[
    fila$columna == columna,
    c("columna", "tipo_declarado", "tipo_inferido", "n", "n_distintos")
  ]
}
rbind(
  cbind(tabla = "padron", clave_de(perfil_padron, "id_persona")),
  cbind(tabla = "visitas", clave_de(perfil_visitas, "id_persona"))
)
#>     tabla    columna tipo_declarado tipo_inferido  n n_distintos
#> 1  padron id_persona         entero        entero  8           8
#> 2 visitas id_persona          texto        entero 20          10

    The registry engine declares id_persona as an integer. The visits engine declares it as text, although the profile, when reading it, infers an integer. It is not a profile error: it is the first sign that the key is not stored the same way on both sides. The visits profile records it as a finding:

    hallazgos(perfil_visitas)[
  hallazgos(perfil_visitas)$columna == "id_persona",
  c("columna", "tipo_hallazgo", "severidad")
]
#>      columna           tipo_hallazgo  severidad
#> 2 id_persona tipo_declarado_distinto sospechoso

    tipo_declarado_distinto does not say that a value is wrong; it says that the text looks like a number. In the registry, the same column is an integer. That is where the cross begins to fail. perfilar_dbi() does not compare the two tables: each call sees a single connection.

    Reading only the keys

    Comparing does not require the whole rows: the keys are enough. And it pays to read them in blocks, so that the memory peak depends on the block rather than on the size of the table. The package does not export a key reader; it is built with DBI::dbSendQuery() and DBI::dbFetch(), the same functions with which perfilar_dbi() reads from the engine.

    leer_por_bloques <- function(conexion, consulta, bloque = 1000) {
  resultado <- DBI::dbSendQuery(conexion, consulta)
  on.exit(DBI::dbClearResult(resultado), add = TRUE)
  partes <- list()
  repeat {
    parte <- DBI::dbFetch(resultado, n = bloque)
    if (!nrow(parte)) break
    partes[[length(partes) + 1L]] <- parte
  }
  if (length(partes)) do.call(rbind, partes) else parte
}

    Here the block is 10 rows so that the walk is visible; in a real table, choose the size by the available memory, not by the number of rows. The visit identifier is read next to the key: it will later serve to locate the orphan rows.

    claves_padron <- leer_por_bloques(
  con_padron, "SELECT id_persona FROM padron ORDER BY id_persona",
  bloque = 10
)
claves_visitas_crudas <- leer_por_bloques(
  con_visitas, "SELECT id_visita, id_persona FROM visitas ORDER BY id_visita",
  bloque = 10
)
data.frame(
  lado = c("padron", "visitas"),
  clase = c(
    class(claves_padron$id_persona),
    class(claves_visitas_crudas$id_persona)
  ),
  ejemplo = c(
    claves_padron$id_persona[[1]],
    claves_visitas_crudas$id_persona[[1]]
  )
)
#>      lado     clase ejemplo
#> 1  padron   integer       1
#> 2 visitas character      01

    The registry arrives with 8 integer keys; the visits, with 20 text keys. The first one in the registry is 1; the first one in the visits, "01". To the eye they are the same person; for the comparison, not yet.

    Comparing in R

    detectar_relaciones() compares 2 data frames in memory. The first table is the reference; the second one depends on it. columnas_candidatas says which pair to compare: without it, the function tries every combination and may find matches that are only similar codes.

    cruce_crudo <- detectar_relaciones(
  claves_padron, claves_visitas_crudas,
  columnas_candidatas = list("id_persona", "id_persona")
)
cruce_crudo[, c(
  "cardinalidad", "n_valores_comunes", "cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1",
  "n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2"
)]
#>        cardinalidad n_valores_comunes cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1 n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2
#> 1 sin_coincidencias                 0                          0                       20

    The coverage of the visits in the registry is 0 %: none of the 20 visit keys matches the 8 keys of the registry. It is not that every person is missing: it is that "01" and 1 are not the same value for the comparison.

    Fixing the shape at the source

    The leading zero is padding, not part of the code. It is fixed in the query, before the value reaches R: this way the key travels with the type that will be compared and the recipe is written in a single place. BIGINT is DuckDB’s name for the integer; each engine has its own.

    claves_visitas <- leer_por_bloques(
  con_visitas,
  paste(
    "SELECT id_visita, CAST(id_persona AS BIGINT) AS id_persona",
    "FROM visitas ORDER BY id_visita"
  ),
  bloque = 10
)
cruce <- detectar_relaciones(
  claves_padron, claves_visitas,
  columnas_candidatas = list("id_persona", "id_persona")
)
cruce[, c(
  "cardinalidad", "n_valores_comunes", "cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1",
  "n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2"
)]
#>   cardinalidad n_valores_comunes cobertura_tabla2_en_tabla1 n_filas_huerfanas_tabla2
#> 1          1:m                 8                        0.9                        2

    Now the coverage is 90 %: 18 of the 20 visits find their person. There remain 2 orphan visits, the ones of people 9 and 10, who are not in the registry.

    huerfanas <- cruce$huerfanas_tabla2[[1]]
data.frame(
  total = huerfanas$total,
  mostradas = huerfanas$mostrados,
  estado = huerfanas$estado,
  alcance = huerfanas$alcance
)
#>   total mostradas     estado  alcance
#> 1     2         2 disponible completo
claves_visitas$id_visita[huerfanas$indices_fila]
#> [1] 19 20

    The trace does not publish the key values; it publishes the row positions. With id_visita read next to the key, those positions translate to visits 19 and 20. In a large table, the read order has to be stable for the position to keep working: that is why the query carries ORDER BY.

    From the comparison to the metric

    A loose coverage is useful for this delivery. Comparing deliveries requires a measure with a name, a date and an identifier. ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad measures the proportion of non-missing keys of the second entity that exist in the first one.

    nucleo <- metricas_nucleo()
regla <- instanciar(
  especializar(
    nucleo$ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad,
    nombre_especifico = "VisitaTienePersona"
  ),
  entidad = c("padron", "visitas"),
  atributos = c("id_persona", "id_persona")
)
medicion <- medir(
  modelo(regla),
  list(padron = claves_padron, visitas = claves_visitas),
  id_medicion = "cruce-2026-01",
  fecha = "2026-01-31"
)
medicion[, c("metrica_especifica", "objeto_medible", "resultado")]
#>   metrica_especifica                          objeto_medible resultado
#> 1 VisitaTienePersona visitas$id_persona -> padron$id_persona       0.9

    The metric returns a single row: the coverage of the foreign key, with the rule name, the dependent entity and the object measured. The id_medicion and the fecha are what make it possible to compare this run with the next one. An NA in the foreign key does not count as an orphan: it is not a value that was looked up, so it does not enter the denominator.

    The metric does not normalize anything. If it is passed the raw keys, it measures 0 %, which is the correct figure for that shape. The correction is made earlier, in the query, and applied to both sides.

    When the keys do not have the same shape

    The visits case was a leading zero. There are 2 more that show up often: uppercase and edge spaces. The in-memory comparison ignores neither.

    codigos_a <- data.frame(codigo = c("A-01", "B-02", " C-03"))
codigos_b <- data.frame(codigo = c("a-01", "b-02", "c-03"))
comparar <- function(a, b) {
  detectar_relaciones(
    a, b, columnas_candidatas = list("codigo", "codigo")
  )$n_valores_comunes
}
c(
  crudo = comparar(codigos_a, codigos_b),
  normalizado = comparar(
    data.frame(codigo = toupper(trimws(codigos_a$codigo))),
    data.frame(codigo = toupper(trimws(codigos_b$codigo)))
  )
)
#>       crudo normalizado 
#>           0           3

    Text versus number is not a problem of classes, but of spelling. An integer and a double with the same integer value match, and a text "1" matches the number 1; but "01", "1.0" or " 1" do not. The comparison uses the exact identity of the value: it neither trims spaces nor changes case. The same happens with dates: "2026-01-31" matches a Date, but "31/01/2026" does not.

    The decision of which shape is canonical belongs to the data, not to the package. If the leading zero is padding, remove it on read; if it is part of the code, restore it on both sides. If case does not distinguish, normalize both tables with the same function; if it does, normalizing would be an error. And if the spaces are accidental, trim them on both sides. What you cannot do is fix only one side and call the result coverage.

    What the package does not do

    It does not join two connections in a single query. perfilar_dbi(), medir_dbi(), perfilar_coleccion() and relaciones_coleccion() receive one connection or one collection; detectar_relaciones() and medir() compare data frames in R. That is the boundary: each engine profiles and projects its own side, and R brings the keys together.

    If the two tables were in the same database, medir_dbi() could resolve the rule in the engine, through the sql_dedicado_referencial path. With two connections there is no query that sees both, and that is why the recipe brings the keys over. That bounded read also protects the data: the full rows do not travel, only the identifiers needed for the comparison.

    Neither does it normalize for you: the comparison is exact. And it does not decide whether a relationship is a real foreign key. Coverage is evidence; the data dictionary and the engine constraints are what confirm it. Coverage is computed over every key it is given: there is no implicit sample that could align with the data. If a subset is read, the coverage is of that subset and that has to be said.

    The two reads are from different moments. If the databases change between them, the coverage mixes two snapshots: it pays to read the keys as close together as possible and record the run date, as is done with the metric.

    Summary

    • perfilar_dbi() describes each table in its engine. The declared type of the key and the tipo_declarado_distinto finding warn when the two sides are not written the same way.
    • Reading only the keys and in blocks bounds the memory peak: dbSendQuery() + dbFetch(n) walk the table without bringing the full rows.
    • detectar_relaciones() measures coverage in the 2 directions and names the orphan rows; medir() with ReglaIntegridadInterEntidad turns it into a measure with a date and an identifier.
    • The comparison is exact: leading zeros, uppercase and spaces are distinct values. Normalizing both sides with the same rule, or fixing the type in the query, is part of the recipe.
    • The package does not cross two connections in a single query: each database is read separately and R is the meeting point.

DBI::dbDisconnect(con_visitas, shutdown = TRUE)
